open_obligations: Read p14 L47-51 to check whether the authors say their absolute accuracies are not comparable to Parrish et al.'s
Note that Parrish et al.'s judges had 90 seconds of passage access, while Michael et al.'s judges never see the passage
Compare question sampling: Michael et al. keep only Gutenberg QuALITY-hard questions needing more than one or two sentences of context
out.other_title: Single debate-style arguments were not found to improve human accuracy in the authors' long-context multiple-choice QA set-up
out.rationale: Both studies ask whether debate helps human judges answer QuALITY reading comprehension questions. Michael et al. restate Parrish et al.'s result that debate does not significantly improve judge accuracy and list differences between the two settings, first that their own debates are unbounded in length, which they suggest may have produced more useful and informative arguments. The passages show no contrary result, so the link records the same question asked in different settings.
out.scope: proposed SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING: Whether debate improves human judge accuracy on hard QuALITY questions; the settings differ in protocol: Michael et al.'s debates are unbounded in length, whereas the linked Parrish et al. study uses single-turn arguments for a preselected correct and a preselected incorrect answer, written by humans familiar with the context, with no refutation (Michael et al. describe Parrish et al.'s one- and two-turn debates as bounded at a single refutation)

text: The authors note that in Parrish et al.'s one- and two-turn debate experiments on QuALITY, debate did not significantly improve judge accuracy, and they point to differences from their own setting. The first is that their debates have unbounded length, so debaters must keep defending their claims, which the authors suggest may produce more useful and informative arguments.
title: Parrish et al. found no significant debate gain on QuALITY in one- and two-turn debates
